title: The Morning Star of the Reformation
subtitle: The Reformation — Lesson 1
description: Meet John Wycliffe, the Morning Star of the Reformation, who translated the Bible into English and inspired the Lollard movement — and Jan Hus, the Bohemian priest whose martyrdom lit the fires of reform.
reviewQuestions: What was John Wycliffe's central conviction about the authority of Scripture, and why was it revolutionary?
Why did Wycliffe believe it was essential to translate the Bible into English?
How did Wycliffe's teachings influence Jan Hus, and what happened at the Council of Constance?
activity: Create a timeline of Pre-Reformation events from 1320 to 1415, including the major dates of Wycliffe's life, his English Bible translation, and the martyrdom of Jan Hus. Illustrate with drawings and write a one-paragraph reflection.

title: Here I Stand — Martin Luther
subtitle: The Reformation — Lesson 2
description: Discover how a German monk's spiritual crisis led to the rediscovery of justification by faith, the posting of the Ninety-Five Theses, and a stand at the Diet of Worms that changed the world.
reviewQuestions: What spiritual crisis tormented Luther, and how did Romans 1:17 resolve it?
What were the Ninety-Five Theses, and why did they spread so rapidly?
What did Luther say at the Diet of Worms, and why is it so important?
activity: Write a first-person journal entry as if you were Martin Luther on the evening after the Diet of Worms, April 18, 1521. Describe the events, your feelings, your courage, and what you expect next. At least 200 words.

title: The Theologian of Geneva — John Calvin
subtitle: The Reformation — Lesson 3
description: Meet John Calvin, the systematic theologian whose Institutes of the Christian Religion and work in Geneva shaped the Reformed tradition and influenced Western civilization for centuries.
reviewQuestions: What was Calvin's 'sudden conversion,' and how did it change his life?
What is the central theme of Calvin's theology in the Institutes?
How did Calvin's Geneva and the Geneva Academy influence Reformed theology across Europe?
activity: Create a two-column comparison chart of Martin Luther and John Calvin — backgrounds, theological emphases, major writings, and legacies. Write a concluding paragraph on one similarity and one difference.

title: God's Outlaw — William Tyndale
subtitle: The Reformation — Lesson 4
description: Follow William Tyndale's heroic quest to translate the Bible into English — from his famous vow to the plowboy, through years as a fugitive, to his martyrdom and the prayer that was answered within three years.
reviewQuestions: Why was translating the Bible into English so dangerous in Tyndale's time?
What was Tyndale's famous statement about the plowboy, and how did he fulfill it?
What were Tyndale's last words, and how were they answered?
activity: Compare a King James Bible passage with Tyndale's original translation side by side. Highlight identical phrases and write a short essay on Tyndale's influence on the KJV.

title: The Thundering Scot — John Knox
subtitle: The Reformation — Lesson 5
description: Travel to Scotland to meet John Knox — galley slave, exile, student of Calvin, and fiery preacher whose iron will brought the Reformation to an entire nation and founded Scottish Presbyterianism.
reviewQuestions: How did George Wishart's martyrdom influence Knox's life and ministry?
What was the significance of the Scottish Parliament's actions in 1560?
What is Presbyterian church government, and how did Knox's Book of Discipline shape it?
activity: Stage a mock debate between John Knox and Mary Queen of Scots. Each participant prepares at least three arguments based on historical positions. Discuss what principles were at stake.

title: The Swiss Reformation — Zwingli and the Radicals
subtitle: The Reformation — Lesson 6
description: Explore the parallel reformation in Switzerland — Zwingli's preaching revolution in Zurich, the tragic failure at the Marburg Colloquy, and the radical Anabaptist movement that pushed reform to its limits.
reviewQuestions: How did Zwingli's approach to preaching represent a departure from medieval practice?
What was the core disagreement between Luther and Zwingli at Marburg?
Who were the Anabaptists, and how did their beliefs differ from other reformers?
activity: Create a Venn diagram comparing Lutheran, Reformed, and Anabaptist traditions. Include at least four points in each section, covering shared and distinctive beliefs.

title: The English Reformation — From Henry VIII to Elizabeth
subtitle: The Reformation — Lesson 7
description: Trace the turbulent English Reformation through four monarchs — Henry VIII's political break with Rome, Edward VI's Protestant reforms, Bloody Mary's persecutions, and Elizabeth's Settlement that gave rise to the Puritans.
reviewQuestions: What political event triggered the English Reformation, and how did it differ from Luther and Calvin?
What were Cranmer's major contributions, and what happened to him under Mary I?
What was the Elizabethan Settlement, and why did it give rise to the Puritans?
activity: Create a 'Monarchs of the English Reformation' chart for Henry VIII, Edward VI, Mary I, and Elizabeth I — dates, religious policy, key actions, and major figures. Write a concluding paragraph on how rapid changes affected ordinary people.

title: The Counter-Reformation and the Council of Trent
subtitle: The Reformation — Lesson 8
description: Examine how the Roman Catholic Church responded to the Protestant challenge — through the Council of Trent's doctrinal definitions, the founding of the Jesuits, and the reinvigorated Inquisition.
reviewQuestions: What were the key doctrinal decisions of the Council of Trent, and how did they respond to Protestant theology?
Who was Ignatius of Loyola, and how did the Jesuits serve the Counter-Reformation?
What methods did the Counter-Reformation use to halt Protestantism? Which were effective?
activity: Create a comparison chart of Reformation and Counter-Reformation — Protestant principles vs. Catholic responses from Trent. Write a paragraph on what the debate reveals about central questions of the faith.

title: The Reformation's Legacy — Creeds, Confessions, and Catechisms
subtitle: The Reformation — Lesson 9
description: Survey the great confessions and catechisms that codified Reformation theology — from the Augsburg Confession and Heidelberg Catechism to the Westminster Standards that defined the Puritan tradition.
reviewQuestions: What purposes do confessions of faith serve in the life of the church?
What is the opening question and answer of the Westminster Shorter Catechism, and why is it significant?
How do the Heidelberg Catechism and Westminster Shorter Catechism differ in their opening emphases?
activity: Memorize the first three questions and answers of the Westminster Shorter Catechism. Write a one-page reflection explaining what they mean and how they apply to daily life.

title: The Reformation's Children — The Puritans and Beyond
subtitle: The Reformation — Lesson 10
description: Trace the Reformation's legacy forward into the Puritan movement, the English Civil War, the Great Ejection, and the modern world — showing that the Reformation was not an end but a beginning.
reviewQuestions: Who were the Puritans, and why did they believe further reform was necessary?
How did the English Civil War affect the Puritan movement?
What are the most important lasting legacies of the Reformation for the modern world?
activity: Write a one-page essay titled 'The Reformation's Greatest Legacy,' arguing for the single most important contribution of the Reformation. Support with specific examples and names from all ten lessons.

title: The Moral Law — Foundation of Christian Ethics
subtitle: Christian Ethics — Lesson 1
description: Begin the study of Christian ethics with the three uses of the law — civil, pedagogical, and normative — and the Puritan conviction that the Ten Commandments are a guide to grateful obedience, not a burden.
reviewQuestions: What are the three uses of the law as taught by Calvin and the Westminster Standards?
How does Jesus show that the law addresses inward attitudes, not just outward actions?
How does Jesus summarize the moral law in two commandments?
activity: Write out the Ten Commandments, organize them into two tablets, and for each write one sentence on the duty required and one on the sin forbidden. This will serve as a reference for the unit.

title: No Other Gods — The First and Second Commandments
subtitle: Christian Ethics — Lesson 2
description: Examine the first two commandments — the foundation of all morality — addressing who we worship (God alone) and how we worship (according to His Word alone), with Calvin's warning that the heart is a factory of idols.
reviewQuestions: What is the difference between the first commandment (who we worship) and the second (how we worship)?
What are some modern forms of idolatry the Puritans would have identified?
What is the Regulative Principle of Worship, and why did the Puritans consider it important?
activity: Conduct a personal 'idol inventory' — list the top five things that occupy your time, thoughts, and affection, and honestly assess whether any displaces God. Write a reflective paragraph.

title: Hallowed Be Thy Name — The Third Commandment
subtitle: Christian Ethics — Lesson 3
description: Study the third commandment's protection of God's sacred name — from profanity and perjury to hypocrisy and irreverent theology — and learn to speak the most powerful name in the universe with the reverence it deserves.
reviewQuestions: What does it mean to take God's name 'in vain'? Identify at least three ways.
Why did the Puritans consider hypocrisy a violation of the third commandment?
What is the positive duty required by the third commandment?
activity: For one full day, pay attention to how God's name is used in media and conversations. Keep a log and write a reflection on what it reveals about our culture's attitude toward the sacred.

title: Remember the Sabbath — The Fourth Commandment
subtitle: Christian Ethics — Lesson 4
description: Complete the first tablet of the law with the fourth commandment — the gift of Sabbath rest, public worship, and spiritual renewal that reveals human beings are made for worship, not merely for labor.
reviewQuestions: What is the theological foundation of the Sabbath as described in Exodus 20:11?
What are the three essential aspects of Sabbath observance as the Puritans understood them?
How does the fourth commandment address social justice?
activity: Design a 'Sabbath Plan' for your family — an ideal Lord's Day schedule including rest, worship, and family devotion. Identify steps for protecting the day from work and digital distractions.

title: Honor and Authority — The Fifth Commandment
subtitle: Christian Ethics — Lesson 5
description: Cross from the first tablet to the second with the fifth commandment — the bridge commandment that establishes the principle of honor and authority governing all human relationships, from family to church to state.
reviewQuestions: Why does the Westminster Catechism extend the fifth commandment beyond parents to all legitimate authority?
What duties does the fifth commandment place on those in authority?
What happens when human authority commands something contrary to God's law?
activity: Map the authority structures in your life — family, church, school, community. For each relationship, write one duty you owe and one duty owed to you. Reflect on how the fifth commandment shapes these relationships.

title: The Sanctity of Life — The Sixth Commandment
subtitle: Christian Ethics — Lesson 6
description: Study the sixth commandment's comprehensive ethic of life — from the prohibition of murder to the duty of preserving life in all its dimensions, grounded in the infinite dignity of every person made in God's image.
reviewQuestions: What is the theological foundation of the sixth commandment? Why does the image of God make life sacred?
How does Jesus deepen the sixth commandment in the Sermon on the Mount?
What three levels of life preservation does Watson identify?
activity: Read Westminster Larger Catechism Q135-136, then write a modern case study involving the sixth commandment and analyze it using today's principles.

title: Purity and Faithfulness — The Seventh Commandment
subtitle: Christian Ethics — Lesson 7
description: Examine the seventh commandment's protection of the marriage covenant and its call to purity of heart — with the Puritans' practical strategies of cultivating strong marriages, avoiding temptation, and maintaining accountability.
reviewQuestions: Why did the Puritans hold marriage in such high regard, against the medieval elevation of celibacy?
How does Jesus deepen the seventh commandment in the Sermon on the Mount?
What three practical strategies did the Puritans recommend for cultivating purity?
activity: Read Genesis 39 and write a character analysis of Joseph, focusing on the qualities that enabled him to resist temptation. Apply his example to modern moral challenges.

title: Justice and Generosity — The Eighth Commandment
subtitle: Christian Ethics — Lesson 8
description: Explore the eighth commandment's comprehensive ethic of property, labor, and stewardship — from the prohibition of theft to the duties of honest work, fair dealing, and generous giving.
reviewQuestions: How does the doctrine of divine ownership shape the understanding of the eighth commandment?
Why did the Puritans identify laziness as a form of theft?
Summarize the three principles of Puritan economic ethics: gain, save, give.
activity: Design a personal or family budget using Puritan principles — dividing income into necessities, savings, and giving. Write a paragraph explaining how stewardship principles shaped your allocations.

title: Truth and Integrity — The Ninth Commandment
subtitle: Christian Ethics — Lesson 9
description: Study the ninth commandment's protection of truth — from perjury and slander to flattery and gossip — and the active duty to pursue truth and defend our neighbor's reputation in an age of misinformation.
reviewQuestions: Why was the ninth commandment so important in ancient Israelite justice? How do the Puritans expand it?
What is the difference between slander, gossip, and backbiting?
What positive duties does the ninth commandment require beyond not lying?
activity: Keep a 'truth journal' for one day, recording every situation involving truth and falsehood. Write a reflective essay on the pervasiveness of temptation to dishonesty and the cost of commitment to truth.

title: The Heart of the Matter — The Tenth Commandment
subtitle: Christian Ethics — Lesson 10
description: Conclude the Ten Commandments with the tenth — the commandment that bypasses behavior to address the hidden desires of the heart, revealing that God demands not merely right actions but right desires, and that contentment in Him is the cure for covetousness.
reviewQuestions: Why is the tenth commandment unique among the Ten Commandments?
How did the tenth commandment expose Paul's sinfulness and drive him to Christ?
What is the Puritan remedy for covetousness?
activity: Write a capstone essay (300-500 words) titled 'The Heart of the Law,' arguing that the Ten Commandments are ultimately about the heart. Reference at least five commandments and conclude with a personal reflection.
